name: Face With Thermometer
baseMeaning: Face with a thermometer in mouth signaling sickness or fever.
tldr: 🤒 is the general get-well emoji for saying “I’m sick” or offering comfort, often with a playful or literal tone.

contextMeanings.meaning: 🤒 can directly report feeling unwell, especially when the sender believes they have a fever.
🤒 is the familiar shorthand for a general get-well wish rather than a precise medical complaint.
With a partner, 🤒 can turn a minor illness into an intimate request for attention and comfort.
🤒 can function as the official-feeling signal that someone is calling out sick.

platformNotes.note: In iMessage, 🤒 often appears between close friends or family members who already know its casual get-well meaning. A warm private conversation gives it more room than a formal workplace thread would.
On Instagram, a public “feel better 🤒” can look like a generic reaction because the sender cannot tailor it as closely. A sentence can make a serious update clearer.

In WhatsApp family groups, 🤒 is easy to recognize as a get-well gesture, though older recipients may still take the thermometer literally. Pairing it with words helps when the illness is more than a passing cold.
In Slack, an emoji-only 🤒 can leave coworkers unsure whether someone is reporting illness or joking about it. “I’m sick today” makes the message clearer without changing its casual tone.

generationalNotes.note: Younger users often meet 🤒 as familiar chat shorthand for being sick or sending a get-well message. The literal thermometer is usually understood as part of the joke.
Some Gen X readers know the get-well shorthand, while others may still hear the literal image of someone being checked for a fever. Familiarity with casual emoji use matters more here than age alone.
A boomer recipient who knows 🤒 only as a face with a thermometer may miss the casual sympathy behind it. In that case, “I hope you feel better” is safer.

warnings.title: Too small for severe illness
warnings.description: Sending 🤒 after surgery, a serious diagnosis, a parent’s death, or another grave development can make your response sound as if you think the person has a cold. Send 🫂, 🤍, or a sincere sentence instead.

warnings.title: Confusing a cold with general illness
warnings.description: 🤒 covers general sickness, but sending it for sneezing or a specific cold may make the message feel off. Use 🤧 when the cold or sneezing is the point.

seoDescription: What does 🤒 mean? It signals general illness, offers a get-well wish, or adds playful sick day energy, but can feel too casual for serious illness.

longForm.overview:
People who know everyday chat shorthand read 🤒 as the quick, general get-well emoji. Its meaning varies more with familiarity than with a clean age line: someone who has seen it in casual messages hears “I’m sick” or “feel better,” while a less familiar reader may focus on the thermometer and hear a literal symptom report. In a joke such as “I’m dying 🤒,” it lets the sender admit they are sick without sounding too serious.

That makes 🤒 broad rather than medically precise. 🤧 points to sneezing or a cold; 🤒 covers anything from a sore throat to a vague day of feeling bad. It also adapts to the relationship: a coworker uses it to report being out sick, a friend sends it with sympathy, and a partner can use it to ask for comfort. Its simplicity is also its weakness. For a cold, it fits. For surgery, serious family illness, or grief, it can make the moment sound shockingly small, so a sentence, 🫂, or 🤍 is usually better.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
Most often, 🤒 follows a plain update: “feeling gross today” or “I’m dying 🤒.” It softens self-disclosure with self-deprecating humor without pretending the illness is trivial. A friend sending “feel better soon 🤒” is offering sympathy in the simplest familiar form, especially in a close chat where the emoji already carries the get-well meaning.

It also shows up when people announce an absence from work: “out sick today, back tomorrow” reads like the official version of calling in sick. With a partner, the same emoji can shift into affection: “cuddle me 🤒” asks for closeness and care. The speaker may genuinely feel unwell, but the face adds a little drama or playfulness.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
Skip 🤒 when the illness is severe. After surgery, it can sound like you think the person has a cold; during a serious family crisis, it can make their experience look trivial. A sincere sentence, 🫂, or 🤍 carries concern without reducing the event to a symptom emoji. Do the same after a parent’s death, when even a cheerful get-well reaction feels misplaced.

The thermometer can also be misunderstood by readers who know the emoji mainly as a literal image rather than casual shorthand. For a specific cold, 🤧 is clearer. When the situation is serious or ambiguous, spelling out “I’m sorry you’re dealing with this—I’m here” usually does more than 🤒 alone.
longForm.howToReply:
If someone sends 🤒 and you want to match the feeling, mirror it with 🤒, send 🫂 for comfort, or use 🤍 to show that you are thinking of them. For a close friend in a serious moment, the 💕🫂 combination adds stronger affection without pretending the illness is trivial. In a genuinely difficult situation, 😢🙏 can combine care with prayer.

When the wording is ambiguous, a sentence is safer than an emoji. “I’m so sorry, I’m here” directly expresses support. If the person’s illness is mild, a short reply such as “rest and drink water” can keep the conversation useful. If 🤒 lands on your own message, add words that explain whether you are genuinely sick, joking, or asking for care.

faqs.question: What does 🤒 mean from a guy?
faqs.answer: It usually means he is sick, possibly with a bit of humor. In a dating context, it can also be an indirect way to ask for attention or affection.

faqs.question: Is 🤒 flirty?
faqs.answer: By itself, 🤒 is mainly a sick or get-well emoji, not a flirty one. It becomes intimate when paired with messages such as “cuddle me” or “come take care of me.”

faqs.question: What does 🤒 mean on TikTok?
faqs.answer: On TikTok, it generally means the speaker feels unwell or is sending someone a get-well wish. The surrounding words determine whether the illness is serious, playful, or exaggerated.

faqs.question: Should I use 🤒 or 🤧 for a cold?
faqs.answer: Use 🤧 when sneezing or a cold is the specific point. Use 🤒 for general sickness, including a fever, sore throat, or vague feeling of being unwell.

conversationExamples.message: ugh i feel awful, not dying but definitely not fine 🤒
conversationExamples.interpretation: The sender is admitting they are sick while making light of it. You can mirror the joke with 🤒 or respond with practical care such as “rest and drink some water.”

conversationExamples.message: i’m sick 😞 can you come cuddle me 🤒
conversationExamples.interpretation: This combines real illness with an intimate request for closeness. A warm reply such as “coming to take care of you” suits the moment better than a medical joke.

conversationExamples.message: taking today off, i’ll be back tomorrow 🤒
conversationExamples.interpretation: The emoji works as a simple out-sick signal. Keep any work reply practical, such as “hope you feel better soon—see you when you’re back.”

conversationExamples.message: still feeling pretty rough, so please don’t send anyone over 🤒
conversationExamples.interpretation: The sender is asking for space while making the update less severe with self-deprecating humor. Reply with concern and reassurance rather than treating the emoji as a joke.

conversationExamples.message: feeling a bit off today but nothing serious 🤒
conversationExamples.interpretation: This is a vague report of general illness, not necessarily a cold. A simple “hope you rest and feel better soon” matches the understated tone.
